newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. to press Bosnian Croats to let Moslems return.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to press Bosnian Croats to let Moslems return.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency said it would press Bosnian Croat authorities on Tuesday to allow back some 300 Moslems expelled over the weekend by a drunken Croatian mob in the town of Jajce.

UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said that the return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people to areas of Bosnia where they were among the ethnic minority was crucial to the success of the 1995 Dayton peace accord.
But she conceded that most of the "easy returns" had already taken place and it would be increasingly tough for the 800,000 internally displaced and 700,000 Bosnians abroad to go home.
"UNHCR has sent an official to Jajce today to try to reverse the appalling expulsions of around 300 Moslems over the weekend by a drunken Croatian mob," O'Toole told a news briefing.
"Our protection officer in the area will be talking to the local authorities in Jajce to try to persuade them to allow people back and to ensure that they are adequately protected."
Bosnian television reported at the weekend that one man had been burned to death when his house was torched near Jajce, whose population is around 98 percent Bosnian Croat.
Under the Dayton pact which ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war, all refugees in the former Yugoslavia have the right to return to their pre-war homes.
"The issue of minority returns is crucial to the Dayton peace process -- it is imperative that they are allowed to continue if the process is to survive," O'Toole said.

About 27,000 people have returned to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation to areas controlled by their former foes where they form an ethnic minority. Between 1,200 and 1,500 have gone to the Serb entity, Republika Srpska, O'Toole said.

On Sunday, the last 85 Moslems of hundreds who had returned to the Jajce area, about 100 km (60 miles) northwest of Sarajevo in central Bosnia, left their village after a weekend of threats and intimidation from local Bosnian Croats.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), which has projected that some 200,000 Bosnians would go home in 1997, estimates that 65,000 had done so by July.
"We are expecting much larger numbers will be repatriating in July and August. Summer is a more traditional time for returns," O'Toole said.
An estimated 80 per cent of the 260,000 Bosnian refugees in Germany come from minority areas of Bosnia, according to UNHCR.
